lesson.title: Big problems, good answers
lesson.subtitle: Local search, knowing when to stop, and leading a project

video.title: Big problems, good answers
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — education lecturer (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph in front of an empty classroom; desk cards spread on a table; a counter spinning up huge numbers.
scenes.animation: The counter spins past millions; Joseph scratches his head.
scenes.narration: Twelve pupils, twelve desks. That’s four hundred and seventy-nine million different seating plans. For a class of forty, the number has forty-eight digits. So how does anyone find a good plan?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: big problems, good answers, and how to lead a project that uses them.

scenes.visual: A seating plan; two pupil cards swap places; a cost counter drops.
scenes.animation: Cards swap; the counter ticks down after each kept swap.
scenes.narration: When there are too many plans to check, start with any plan and improve it in small steps. Swap two pupils; if the plan gets better, keep the swap. Repeat until no swap helps. That’s local search, or hill climbing.

scenes.visual: A bar chart of where eight hill-climbing runs stopped.
scenes.animation: Bars rise one by one; the two runs at 37 turn green.
scenes.narration: The catch: it can get stuck. A plan no single swap improves is only the best nearby, like a valley that isn’t the lowest. In the seating lab, hill climbing stops anywhere from thirty-seven to forty-seven, and finds thirty-seven about one run in four.

scenes.visual: Two columns: hill climbing (only better swaps) and annealing (some worse swaps while hot).
scenes.animation: A ball rolls into a valley and stops; a second ball bounces out and settles deeper.
scenes.narration: Simulated annealing accepts some worse swaps on purpose: often while it’s hot, rarely as it cools. Early on, that lets it climb out of a valley and find a deeper one. In the lab, it reaches thirty-seven about two runs in three.

scenes.animation: Lines type; the line with exp highlights.
scenes.narration: Its rule fits in a few lines. A worse swap is kept with a chance that shrinks the worse it is, and as the temperature falls.

scenes.visual: A stopwatch and a ruler between ‘best found 37’ and ‘bound 35’.
scenes.animation: The ruler measures the gap; ‘about 5%’ appears.
scenes.narration: Big problems rarely come with a proof of the best. So decide what good enough means before you start: a time limit, and a gap. If you know no plan can cost less than thirty-five and you’ve found thirty-seven, you’re within about five percent.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah points to a seating plan with ‘41’ on it. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Hill climbing stopped at forty-one, and no single swap improves it. Is forty-one the best plan?

scenes.visual: Several runs from different starting plans, each ending at a different cost.
scenes.animation: Run lines draw and settle at different heights.
scenes.narration: Not necessarily: it’s only the best nearby. Run it again from other starts, or let annealing escape, and compare the results.

scenes.visual: A project board with four columns, cards moving from left to right.
scenes.animation: Each step’s card slides into place as it is said.
scenes.narration: Now the part no solver does: leading the project. Start from the problem and the people it affects, and agree the goal and the fairness rules with them. Collect the data, build a small model, and test it on last year’s plan. Pilot it, explain it, and decide together.

scenes.visual: A teacher reviewing the plan with a pen; a small ‘appeal’ box on the noticeboard.
scenes.animation: The pen adds a change; a note drops into the appeal box.
scenes.narration: Keep a person in charge of the final call, with a way to appeal. A teacher who can’t come on Fridays is a rule the data never knew. And publish how the plan was made.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: twelve desks, lines between pupils, a cost chart going down.
scenes.animation: A finger presses Run; the cost line jumps, then settles.
scenes.narration: In the app, seat twelve pupils. Run hill climbing a few times, then annealing, and change the starting temperature.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside a laptop showing ‘gap 2%’ and a calendar showing tomorrow. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The exam rota solver has run for an hour. It’s within two percent of the bound, and the deadline is tomorrow. Do you keep it running?

scenes.visual: Four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Two percent is good enough for a rota due tomorrow: stop, check, explain. Remember: local search improves step by step, and can get stuck. Annealing accepts some worse moves to escape. Decide good enough in advance, and keep people in charge.

scenes.visual: Pupils at the board moving name cards between desk boxes; a cost tally beside it.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: draw the seating plan on the board, with names on cards. Pupils swap two cards at a time, keeping a swap only if the plan gets better. When they’re stuck, allow one worse swap, and see if they do better.

checkpoints.prompt: Hill climbing stopped at 41, and no single swap improves it. Is 41 the best plan?

options.text: No: hill climbing is always wrong
Not necessarily: it may be stuck in a valley

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — no single swap helps, so it’s the best nearby. Other starts, or annealing, may find a deeper valley.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — “no swap helps” means best nearby, not best overall. In the lab, 37 is possible.

checkpoints.prompt: The exam rota solver is within 2% of the bound, and the rota is due tomorrow. Keep it running?

options.text: Yes: run until it proves the best
No: 2% is good enough here; check it with people

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 2% from the bound is very close. The time is better spent checking the rota with the people who will use it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — at most 2% could still be gained, maybe nothing. Stop, check the rota with people and explain it.
